title: Phaal
subtitle: The hottest British Indian restaurant curry
excerpt: Phaal is a British Indian restaurant creation and is considered the hottest curry available in Indian restaurants in the UK. It is made with a tomato and onion base cooked with enormous quantities of ground chilli and chilli powder, producing a sauce that is intensely hot and deeply flavoured. It is very spicy.
sourceNotes: Phaal was created in British Indian restaurants in the late 20th century as an extreme heat challenge. It is not a traditional Indian dish but a BIR (British Indian Restaurant) invention. Birmingham is particularly associated with phaal, though the dish appears on menus throughout the UK.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes well. The heat mellows slightly on freezing and reheating.

content.text: Phaal is an extreme curry. The heat level puts it well beyond vindaloo. The sauce is made from a tomato and onion base loaded with bird's eye chillies, scotch bonnets, and large quantities of chilli powder. Use chicken or lamb. Serve with plain basmati rice and plenty of raita: the yoghurt is the only effective relief from the heat.

items.prepNote: bird's eye or small hot red chillies, sliced
pure chilli powder, not a blend

content.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy pan over high heat. Add the onions and fry for 8 to 10 minutes until deep golden brown. Add the garlic and ginger and cook for 2 minutes.
Add all the chillies (fresh, dried flakes, and chilli powder) along with the cumin, coriander, and turmeric. Stir over high heat for 2 minutes. Open a window.
Add the tinned tomatoes with a splash of water. Simmer for 15 minutes, stirring, until the oil rises to the surface and the sauce is deeply coloured and reduced.

Add the chicken pieces to the sauce. Stir to coat. Cook over medium-high heat for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring regularly, until the chicken is cooked through and the sauce has thickened around it. Add a splash of water if needed to prevent burning.
Stir in the garam masala. Taste and season with salt. Serve with basmati rice and raita.

items.cause: Fewer chillies were used than the recipe calls for, or the chillies were mild varieties
items.fix: Phaal requires large quantities of very hot chillies, particularly bird's eye and scotch bonnet, to reach the intended heat level.

content.text: Phaal was invented in British Indian restaurants: a challenge dish, the hottest curry on the menu. Some Birmingham restaurants require diners to sign a disclaimer before ordering. The dish is almost unknown in India itself. It belongs entirely to the British Indian restaurant tradition, alongside balti and chicken tikka masala.
